power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Personalizing Structured Self-Help in the Moment: Students' Experiences With Embedded AI Chatbots in a Guided Digital Mental Health Platform

author.affiliation:
Department of Clinical, Neuro and Developmental Psychology
								Amsterdam Public Health research institute
								Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam
								
									1105 1081 HV
									De Boelelaan Amsterdam
									Netherlands

text.text: Background: University students can use guided digital mental health interventions without having immediate access to a coach.
Fixed programme content does not always answer questions about choosing a programme or applying an exercise to a personal situation.
This study examined whether purpose-specific large language model chatbots can address this gap within an existing platform, MoodLift.
The study focused on how students judged their usefulness, trustworthiness, and safety.
Assistant and an AI Coach.
Ten first-year students used both tools.
They completed usability and acceptability measures before joining one of two focus groups.
Questionnaire results were summarized descriptively.
Focus-group transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.
: Mean Chatbot Usability Questionnaire scores were 70.3 for the Program Selection Assistant and 70.8 for the AI Coach.
Acceptability ratings were generally positive.

Five themes were developed: (1) from general self-help to personal support; (2) providing direction while preserving autonomy; (3) students trusted the chatbots conditionally, not automatically; (4) embedding made AI more relevant and legitimate; and (5) safety required a bounded, complementary role.
Situational fit emerged as a cross-cutting principle: preferences varied between students and depended on the task and context.
Conclusions: Purpose-specific chatbots can help students use guided digital self-help at the moment questions arise.
Their value depends on reliable responses and an explicit scope.
Providers should explain how data are handled and who remains responsible, while ensuring that human support is available
Mental health problems are common among university students.

In the WHO World Mental Health International College Student initiative, approximately one third of first-year students screened positive for a common 12-month mental disorder (Auerbach et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In the WHO World Mental Health International College Student initiative, approximately one third of first-year students screened positive for a common 12-month mental disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Auerbach et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Only a minority of affected students had received treatment (Bruffaerts et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Only a minority of affected students had received treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bruffaerts et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Treatment capacity is one part of this gap.
Students also report that they prefer to manage problems themselves or are unsure where to seek help.
Lack of time, stigma, and doubts about treatment create further barriers (Ebert et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Lack of time, stigma, and doubts about treatment create further barriers <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Ebert et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Universities can respond by offering support that is available early and can be used privately, with a route to professional care when needed.
Guided digital self-help can make such support available at scale.
Internet-based interventions have shown small-to-moderate effects on student mental health outcomes (Harrer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Internet-based interventions have shown small-to-moderate effects on student mental health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Harrer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Their public health value is nevertheless determined partly by use: students must start an intervention, continue with it, and apply what they learn.
Reach and sustained engagement vary considerably (Taylor et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Reach and sustained engagement vary considerably <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Taylor et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Students have also expressed preferences concerning personalization and usability and privacy and access to a person remain important (Oti & Pitt, 2021).
text.formatted: Students have also expressed preferences concerning personalization and usability and privacy and access to a person remain important <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Oti & Pitt, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: MoodLift was developed within the Dutch Caring Universities consortium and combines evidence-informed self-help programmes with asynchronous e-coaching (Struijs et al., in press).
text.formatted: MoodLift was developed within the Dutch Caring Universities consortium and combines evidence-informed self-help programmes with asynchronous e-coaching <ref type="bibr">(Struijs et al., in press)</ref>.

text.text: A coach is not continuously available, and fixed content cannot anticipate every question.
Additional support may therefore be useful when students are choosing a programme or working through the programme content and exercises.
It may also help them translate general advice into something they can do next.
Conversational agents offer one possible form of immediate support.
Most research has concerned standalone mental health chatbots.
These systems provide psychoeducation or exercises, and some are intended to offer emotional or treatment-related support.
Meta-analytic findings show benefits for some mental health outcomes, with substantial differences between systems and studies (Li et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic findings show benefits for some mental health outcomes, with substantial differences between systems and studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Li et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Large language models allow a less scripted exchange versus traditional rule-based chatbots.
Clinical evidence for these newer applications is still limited.
A review of 160 mental health chatbot studies documented rapid growth in LLM applications and identified inaccurate responses and privacy concerns.
It also found therapeutic claims that had not been adequately evaluated (Hua et al., 2025).
text.formatted: It also found therapeutic claims that had not been adequately evaluated <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hua et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: More importantly, evidence on standalone chatbots cannot readily answer how a chatbot functions inside already established interventions.
A chatbot embedded in an intervention has a narrower task.
It can help users select, understand, or apply established material between contacts with a coach.
It does not have to deliver a complete intervention.
The small body of relevant research has produced mixed findings.
For example, adding an automated chatbot to internet-based cognitive behavioural therapy increased programme completion among workers with subthreshold depression (Yasukawa et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, adding an automated chatbot to internet-based cognitive behavioural therapy increased programme completion among workers with subthreshold depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Yasukawa et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In another study, natural-language feedback increased weekly participation in a self-guided intervention.
The primary depression outcome did not improve however (So et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The primary depression outcome did not improve however <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(So et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Users of a generative-AI CBT application engaged more often and for longer than users of digital CBT workbooks; reductions in anxiety and depression were comparable (McFadyen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Users of a generative-AI CBT application engaged more often and for longer than users of digital CBT workbooks; reductions in anxiety and depression were comparable <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(McFadyen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These studies indicate that conversation can change how intervention content is used, even when clinical effects do not differ.
The systems, however, vary in technology and intended function.
Their level of integration also differs.
Clinical outcomes provide only part of the evaluation.
An embedded chatbot must be useful for its assigned task, and users must be able to decide how much confidence to place in an answer.
Qualitative research among students and other stakeholders has drawn attention to evidence-based content and user autonomy (Bartali et al., 2026; Reichenpfader et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Qualitative research among students and other stakeholders has drawn attention to evidence-based content and user autonomy <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bartali et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Reichenpfader et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Participants in those studies also wanted understandable information about data and emergency procedures.
They generally described chatbots as complements to human support.

Work on responsible health applications adds questions about the sources used by a model, human oversight, and organizational responsibility (Olisaeloka et al., 2026; World Health Organization, 2024).
text.formatted: Work on responsible health applications adds questions about the sources used by a model, human oversight, and organizational responsibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Olisaeloka et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">World Health Organization, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A university platform could offer relevant content and recognizable human backup.
Whether students trust the platform and its provider remains an empirical question.
Few studies have examined purpose-specific LLM assistants within an existing guided intervention.
We therefore studied two MoodLift prototypes.
The Program Selection Assistant helped students choose a programme from the platform; the AI Coach supported them while they used programme content.
Neither was intended to replace human coaching or professional care.
The research question was: How do students experience the use of AI chatbots within the MoodLift platform, and under which conditions do they consider such applications useful, safe, and trustworthy?
An exploratory qualitative study with two focus groups was conducted.
Usability and acceptability questionnaires provided descriptive information about each prototype.
MoodLift is the guided digital mental health platform of Caring Universities.
Its structured programmes address, among others, low mood and worry, as well as stress, procrastination, perfectionism, sleep, self-esteem, relationships, and substance use.
Trained ecoaches support students while they work through a programme (Struijs et al., in press).
text.formatted: Trained ecoaches support students while they work through a programme <ref type="bibr">(Struijs et al., in press</ref>).

text.text: The prototypes were designed to help with programme selection and questions that arose between coaching contacts.
During the study, students accessed them separately alongside MoodLift; technical integration had not yet taken place.
Both prototypes ran on Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4 (claude-sonnet-4-20250514).
The system prompts instructed the model to ask questions collaboratively and to respect student autonomy.
They also defined professional boundaries and described how to handle uncertainty.
Crisis procedures were included.
The model had not been fine-tuned on MoodLift data.
At inference, it received platform information from the prompts and searchable knowledge bases.
The Program Selection Assistant was called the "Choice Tool" during testing.
It asked about the student's main concerns and explored possible connections between problems before proposing a starting programme from 12 options.
Matching rules and programme descriptions were included in the prompt.
A further 256 indexed fragments from MoodLift materials were available.
Students could ask for an alternative or an explanation and could correct the tool.
The instructions prohibited diagnosis and treatment.
They also prohibited pressure and unsupported inferences.
Messages indicating acute risk led to a referral to professional or emergency support.
Students used the "AI Coach" while working within a self-selected programme.
The Coach used retrieval-augmented generation: it retrieved relevant passages from a knowledge base containing 1,290 fragments, taken from the programme manuals.
It could, for example, explain an exercise, generate examples, or help a student apply the material to their personal situation or experience.
Retrieved content was given priority when it addressed the question.
The instructions stated that the Coach was not a therapist and should not diagnose or give medical advice.
It was also told not to make important decisions for students.
Acute-risk messages activated crisis guidance and referral.
Each prototype responded in the language used by the student.
Ten Dutch-speaking first-year psychology students took part.
Five women and five men; their approximate age was 19 years.
They were recruited through the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam SONA pool.
Eligibility required current student status and a minimum age of 18 years.
Participants also needed sufficient Dutch or English proficiency.
They received course research credits and a €20 bol.com gift card.
Three students attended one focus group and seven attended the other.
Participants first provided digital informed consent and demographic information.
They then received a test account and used the Choice Tool once.
They were asked to enter a real or realistic situation involving several concerns.
The test accounts already required a MoodLift programme to be selected.
This placed the programme recommendation by the Choice Tool within a partly artificial sequence, which was taken into account during the analysis.
Participants next used a selected MoodLift programme and the AI Coach for approximately one week.
Daily login was encouraged.
They could ask for clarification, request examples, or discuss a difficulty they encountered in the programme.
Private reflection notes were encouraged but were not collected.
Participants completed the questionnaires immediately before their focus group.
The groups took place in person at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam on June 17 and 19, 2026, and lasted 89 and 81 minutes.
The author moderated both sessions.
They were conducted in Dutch and audio-recorded for transcription.
English quotations were checked against the Dutch transcripts and then verified from the recordings.
The 16-item Chatbot Usability Questionnaire was administered for each prototype (CUQ; Holmes et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The 16-item Chatbot Usability Questionnaire was administered for each prototype (CUQ; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Holmes et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Items are presented in positive and negative pairs and use a five-point response scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree.
The questionnaire covers the chatbot's purpose and navigation.
Other items address understanding, response quality, error handling, and ease of use.
After reversing negative items, total scores were transformed to a 0-100 scale.
Higher values indicate better usability.
No validated cutoff is available, so the scores were interpreted descriptively (Pavão et al., 2026).
text.formatted: No validated cutoff is available, so the scores were interpreted descriptively <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Pavão et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Four additional items were rated on five-point scales.
They asked about added value and intended use within MoodLift, followed by trust in the information or advice and willingness to recommend the prototype.
"Agree" and "strongly agree" were classified as positive responses.
The semistructured guide first asked about the overall experience and each prototype.
Participants then compared the tools with general-purpose AI.
Later questions concerned trust and safety, possible use in practice, and desired improvements.
The moderator used follow-up questions when students discussed relevance or personalization.
Further prompts covered programme content, motivation, privacy, the provider, and possible human intervention.
Questions about data use and confidence in the advice were also included.
We calculated the mean, standard deviation, and range of each CUQ score.
Additional items were summarized as positive-response counts with percentages.
The sample was not used for inferential tests or formal comparisons between prototypes.
A reflexive thematic analysis was conducted following Braun and Clarke (2006, 2021).
text.formatted: A reflexive thematic analysis was conducted following <ref type="bibr">Braun and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Clarke (2006, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Coding was largely inductive and semantic: initial codes described participants' accounts in relatively concrete terms.
Theme development was more interpretive and was informed by the research question, particularly what participants' accounts implied for the usefulness, trustworthiness, and safety of the chatbots.
The transcripts were read repeatedly and divided into data extracts, which were assigned fine-grained codes.
Coding was iterative: codes were compared and refined first within and subsequently across the two focus groups.
Related codes were then grouped into candidate themes.
These themes were reviewed against both the coded extracts and the complete transcripts, with attention to their internal coherence, boundaries, and potentially contradictory cases.
Themes were revised until each captured a distinct and meaningful pattern in relation to the research question.
Differences between people, tasks, and situations occurred across the themes and were therefore conceptualized as a cross-cutting principle rather than as a separate sixth theme.
Illustrative quotations were selected after reviewing the extracts associated with each theme, considering their clarity, relevance, and ability to represent variation within the data.
The moderator and analyst is a clinical psychologist and researcher.
He leads work on Caring Universities and MoodLift and created the prototypes.
This background made it easier to interpret references to the platform.
It also meant that favourable findings could be personally and professionally welcome.
Before data collection, the researcher expected relatively critical responses because students could compare the prototypes with polished general-purpose chatbots.
Several steps were used to keep the analysis open to other interpretations.
Codes remained linked to their source fragments, uncertainties and counterexamples were documented, and all harmonized codes were reviewed.
Empirical themes were kept separate from suggestions for future design.
Concerns about privacy and security were considered alongside positive accounts of MoodLift.
The analysis also retained criticism of the technical integration and the limits of AI.
OpenAI's ChatGPT was used as a support tool during parts of the qualitative analysis, including code harmonisation, and the exploration of candidate thematic groupings.
AI-assisted outputs were treated as suggestions.
The author reviewed the analysis against the transcript data and made all final coding, thematic, and interpretative decisions.

Five participants were women and five were men.
Their approximate age was 19 years.
All reported regular use of the AI Coach during the test week.
Mean CUQ scores were 70.3 for the Choice Tool and 70.8 for the AI Coach.

CUQ = Chatbot Usability Questionnaire.
CUQ scores range from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better perceived usability.

Results are descriptive; no formal comparison between prototypes was conducted.
Five themes were developed from the focus-group data.
They concerned personal support, guidance that left room for choice, how trust was formed, the effect of embedding, and the limited role students assigned to AI.
The themes together described students' views of usefulness, trustworthiness, and safety.
Preferences did not apply uniformly.
Situational fit was used to describe differences between students and between moments of use.
Students valued the Coach when it made static programme material relevant to their immediate situation.
It adapted examples and explained exercises in different words.
Follow-up questions could bring structure to an experience that was still unclear.
One participant compared the fixed examples in the module with those supplied by the Coach: Continuity increased the practical value of the Coach.
If it seemed to know where a student was in the programme, the conversation could continue without extensive repetition.
Without memory, students had to reconstruct earlier information and the exchange became less personal.
Direct availability was another benefit.
Some participants rarely needed this however, a clear module already gave them enough support.
The Choice Tool was most helpful when it explored a student's concerns before offering direction.
It could connect problems and ask which concern was most disruptive.
This reduced complexity.
Students accepted a recommendation more readily when the preceding questions made sense.
A quick recommendation, by comparison, appeared overly certain.

Students worried that people unfamiliar with AI might assume that all relevant programmes and problems had been considered: "Someone who does not really understand how a chatbot works might think it has genuinely weighed all the options, even though it has not discussed the other problems with you at all."
(FG1, Participant 2)
The concern became more salient when participants imagined using the Choice Tool while distressed or uncertain.
An unsuitable recommendation might feel confronting or send a vulnerable student "down the wrong path" (FG2, Participant 5).
They wanted the tool to explore the problem before narrowing the options.
A brief explanation and the opportunity to correct the recommendation were also important.
Several participants preferred to receive two or three plausible programmes.
The chatbot would still reduce complexity, but the student could compare options.
One participant said: "It felt as though it had already made the decision for you" (FG2, Participant 5).
A single recommendation was acceptable to others, especially when it confirmed what they already expected.
Students' tolerance for direction depended on how the recommendation had been reached and whether they retained the final choice.
Students assessed trust response by response rather than extending it to AI in general.
They looked for competence and realism.
Restraint, consistency with the programme, and an identifiable basis for the information also affected their judgement.
Questions about data handling introduced another consideration.
A confident tone could make a favourable first impression.
Uncertainty about the source could reverse it quickly.
Some participants regarded the MoodLift Coach as more objective than general-purpose AI and less inclined to agree with the user.
They contrasted its professional restraint with chatbots that reassured people too readily.
An uncomfortable answer could therefore remain credible.
One participant said: "It may have been a harsh truth, but it felt realistic" (FG2, Participant 5).
Advice that seemed to have been constructed outside the programme contend weakened trust in the programme grounding.

For example, one participant received a usefullooking breathing exercise that was absent from the programme and questioned the source of other information: The breathing exercise itself was not considered harmful.
Its unclear origin was the problem.
The participant could not tell whether the Coach had retrieved the exercise from MoodLift or generated it independently.
This made it harder to know which other answers needed checking.
Students wanted enough source information to evaluate an answer.
They did not want a technical explanation to interrupt every exchange.
Disclosure also reflected students' beliefs about access to their conversations.

When considering a possible future implementation, one participant said that they would prefer general-purpose ChatGPT if researchers could access conversations with the embedded chatbot (FG1, Participant 1).
Others placed more weight on convenience or were less worried about a data leak.
Across these views, students wanted information about the chatbot to be presented in a concise and layered format.
Key information about its purpose and limitations should be visible upfront, without requiring users to work through lengthy disclaimers or legalistic text.
More detailed information should remain easy to find under clear and relevant headings, including how long data were retained, who could access them, and who was responsible for the system.
Embedding changed how participants understood the prototypes.
Because students accessed them separately (the prototypes were not yet integrated in the platform), several initially missed the connection with MoodLift.
That connection became clearer through use.

When the chatbot drew on the content of the MoodLift programmes, students found its responses more relevant to what they were working on and saw less need to consult a separate, general-purpose chatbot.
Provision through a university also gave the chatbot credibility because the university was associated with expertise, student wellbeing, and non-commercial interests.
However, university provision alone was not sufficient: students still wanted assurance that their data would be protected and that the chatbot would provide reliable responses.
Programme grounding distinguished the Coach from a generic chatbot.
Participants knew that some answers could also be found through an internet search.
The benefit was receiving an answer while they were already working in MoodLift.

The Coach could connect a broad question to programme theory and continue with a relevant follow-up question: "If I asked anything related to self-confidence, it immediately brought in the theory from the programme.
The answer was realistic and applicable, and it asked follow-up questions to help solve it further."
(FG2, Participant 5)
University or psychologically informed provision increased confidence for some participants.
One student preferred MoodLift because "there is a university behind it and psychology behind it" (FG1, Participant 1).
Participants expected a non-commercial provider to give wellbeing greater priority than monetization.
University affiliation was not sufficient by itself.
Memories of university data breaches led them back to the need for demonstrated privacy and technical performance.
Students described the chatbots as immediate additions to a structured programme and its human support.
They did not regard them as replacements for professional or relational care.
Scalable support was attractive when the chatbot's limits were visible.
People were still expected to take responsibility for monitoring and escalation.
Participants saw a possible benefit if repeated difficulties raised in a chat became visible to an e-coach.
Follow-up and responsibility would remain with the person.
They also wanted to distinguish a coach's messages from text generated by AI: Participants also asked what would happen if a conversation revealed severe negative thoughts or an acute crisis.
Intervention seemed acceptable in high-risk situations.
It nevertheless raised questions about who could access messages and when confidentiality might be breached.
One participant accepted intervention "only when someone is genuinely tending toward suicide or harming themselves" (FG1, Participant 2).
Students expected any monitoring to be proportionate and disclosed.
Data access should be restricted, and people should remain responsible for the crisis procedure.
The shortened focus-group guide contained fewer direct questions about safety.
The findings show that students cared about role boundaries and access to human help.
They cannot establish that these were the only safety concerns.
Preferences changed across students and situations.
Some wanted a warm style with emoticons.
Others accepted a robotic tone as long as the information was useful.
The Coach had less value when the programme content was already clear; it became useful when a student was stuck or wanted to apply an exercise personally.
Willingness to disclose information varied with the sensitivity of the topic and beliefs about privacy.
Ideas about authenticity played a part as well.
No single conversational style or level of support suited every person and moment.

text.text: Participants described useful support as personal, actionable, and connected to programme content.
They wanted guidance without losing control of a decision.
Trust was based on credible responses and on understandable information about the system.
For safety, they emphasized limits and access to a person.
Situational fit affected each of these judgements.
Conditions under which embedded AI chatbot support was perceived as useful, trustworthy, and safe.
Note.

Students responded positively to two prototype, purpose-specific chatbots-a programme selection assistant and an in-programme coach-embedded in MoodLift, a guided digital mental health platform for university students.
The Coach was particularly useful when it helped students apply programme content to their own situations.
Students welcomed guidance but wanted to retain control over their decisions.
Trust was conditional on both the quality of individual responses and what students knew about the system, including its information sources, data practices, limitations, and provider.
Students viewed the chatbots as complements to structured self-help and human support rather than as replacements for either.
The AI Coach was valued mainly for translating general material into a personal example or feasible next step.
